claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a low manganese content.
As-received Q235 steel has a heterogeneous grain microstructure.
The as-received microstructure of Q235 predisposes it to form an iron-based oxide film during exposure.
An annealing pretreatment can produce a finer and more uniform grain structure in Q235 steel.
The annealing pretreatment can promote modest manganese segregation in Q235 steel.
Annealing-induced grain refinement and manganese segregation facilitate formation of a more continuous and adherent iron-manganese oxide film during salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
The proposed iron-manganese oxide film may be a spinel-type phase.
Rapid oxidation kinetics at 700–900 °C permit formation of a continuous protective oxide film on Q235 steel.
A coherent iron-manganese oxide film acts as a barrier that retards further corrosive attack.
Oxidation kinetics at room temperature are too slow to form an equivalently protective film on Q235 steel.
Room-temperature salt exposure produces a thinner and more discontinuous oxide layer than high-temperature exposure.
The less protective room-temperature oxide layer results in higher localized corrosion.
Annealed Q235 steel will exhibit lower mass change than as-received Q235 during high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 steel will exhibit a lower corrosion rate than as-received Q235 during high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 steel will form a thicker and more continuous protective oxide film than as-received Q235 during high-temperature salt exposure.
As-received Q235 forms a less continuous and less protective oxide film during high-temperature exposure than annealed Q235.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to low-alloy, low-manganese steels under salt exposure.
The mechanism may not apply to more highly alloyed or specially engineered steels in which other passivation mechanisms predominate.
